name: Henry VII of England
summary: The first Tudor king, who won the crown at Bosworth in 1485 and then consolidated it by marrying Elizabeth of York. He weakened the great lords through bonds, recognisances, statutes against liveries and retainers, and the Star Chamber, and he raised revenue through penal-law forfeitures, benevolences and taxation, pursued by Empson and Dudley. He protected English shipping and trade through navigation statutes and the 1496 Magnus Intercursus, and he arranged dynastic marriages for his children. His own written views are scarce, so most of this record comes from the measures attributed to him and from later chroniclers.

property-fundamental.rationale: Inferred: Bacon describes forfeitures on penal laws, the confiscation of estates and the resumption of crown grants in the reign, which overrode owners' property. No stated view on property rights is recorded.

strong-leader.rationale: Inferred: he ruled through a small council of lawyers and the prerogative Star Chamber, and Bacon describes the king's use of the council's 'censorian power' to bypass ordinary courts. No stated view on strong leadership is recorded.

decide-locally.rationale: Inferred: his reign centralised enforcement in the Council, Star Chamber and bonds on justices of the peace; local justices were kept under crown control. No stated view on local decision-making is recorded.

free-trade.rationale: Mixed evidence: the 1496 Magnus Intercursus restored free commerce with Burgundy, but his Navigation statutes and embargo of 1494 restricted trade. Bacon and Wikipedia record both; no stated view on free trade as a principle is recorded.

experts-over-public.rationale: Inferred: he governed through trained lawyers and clerics such as Morton, Empson and Dudley, whom Bacon calls 'lawyers in science' and privy counsellors; no stated view on experts versus the public is recorded.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Inferred: Bacon describes statutes requiring Gascon wines and woad to be carried in English ships and laws against merchant strangers, which favoured native shipping and commodities. These are protective measures, though not tariffs in the strict sense.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Inferred: the crown took up the alum trade from 1486 and built a dry dock at Portsmouth in 1495, and Bacon describes a navy built as a matter of state power. These are state-directed investments; no stated view on investment policy is recorded.

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Inferred: Bacon reports that the king's title rested on his Lancastrian inheritance, on the marriage to Elizabeth of York and on conquest; the first two are hereditary grounds. No stated view on hereditary monarchy in general is recorded.

military-superiority.rationale: Inferred: Bacon reports the king aimed to make England potent by sea and by land, with a navy and native soldiers rather than mercenaries. No stated view on military rivalry is recorded.

harm-principle.rationale: Inferred: the vagrancy statute suppressed dice, cards, unlawful games and alehouses for servants and the common people, as Bacon describes, without any showing of harm to others. No stated view on the harm principle is recorded.

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: The livery and retainer statutes (3 Hen. VII c.1; 19 Hen. VII c.14) penalised retaining by indenture and giving livery and badges, which is a lord-and-follower bond of the kind this statement describes. The statutes are measures of the reign, and Bacon credits the king with pressing them.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Inferred: Bacon describes the king as accumulating treasure and relying on fines and forfeitures rather than borrowing, and Wikipedia says he stabilised finances. No stated view on stimulus spending is recorded.

work-for-welfare.rationale: No recorded position on welfare conditions; penal vagrancy statutes are something nearby.

ban-interest.rationale: Mixed evidence: Bacon reports anti-usury laws (against excessive interest and 'bastard usury') passed in his parliament, which regulate rather than prohibit lending. The record does not show a view on banning interest outright.

trade-surplus.rationale: Inferred: Bacon reports a law forbidding payment in gold to merchant strangers so that treasure stayed in the realm, and laws favouring native commodities over imports. This is a mercantilist measure; no stated view on the trade balance is recorded.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Inferred: the Star Chamber and attainders against rebels operated outside ordinary common-law process, as Bacon describes. No stated view on suspending legal protections in an emergency is recorded.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: No recorded position on food prices; maximum prices for cloth are something nearby.

death-penalty.rationale: Inferred: Bacon reports executions for treason of pretenders and their supporters, including Perkin Warbeck and the Earl of Warwick in 1499. These were executions for rebellion, not terrorism; no stated view on capital punishment is recorded.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Inferred: Bacon reports the king began to pare the privilege of clergy, so that convicted clerks were branded in the hand. This is a limited curb on clerical privilege; no stated view on church property is recorded.

region-keeps-system.rationale: Poynings' law, which Bacon places in the tenth year of the king's reign, made all English statutes binding in Ireland and subject to English approval, removing Irish legal independence. Bacon writes in 1622, so this is a late secondhand report.

elective-rulers.rationale: Inferred: the king secured the crown by descent through his marriage and settled it on his heirs, not by election among the political nation. No stated view on elective rule is recorded.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Mixed evidence: he sought parliamentary subsidies, yet Bacon reports general benevolences and commissions issued without parliament, and his 1485 proclamation promised to end such exactions except in ancient cases. The record points both ways.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Inferred: Bacon reports executions and attainders of rebels and pretenders and the use of the Star Chamber against armed followings. No stated view on suppressing political opposition as such is recorded.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Inferred: the 1498 letters patent to the Cabots required that the commerce from their discoveries be with England. This is a state claim on the economic benefit of new lands; no stated colonial policy is recorded.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The 1485 Act of Succession settled the crown's inheritance on his line, and his marriages (Elizabeth of York, Arthur to Catherine of Aragon, Margaret to James IV) were made to pass the crown to his heirs; he made Henry VIII heir after Arthur died in 1502.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Inferred: the Star Chamber punished offences 'after their demerits' rather than under fixed standing rules, and Bacon describes forfeitures on penal laws pursued case by case. No stated view on rule by standing law is recorded.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: The 1487 Star Chamber Act (3 Hen. VII c.1) and the 1504 livery statute (19 Hen. VII c.14) targeted private liveries, retainers and armed maintenance of great men; Bacon says the king recommended the 1487 measures. These laws restricted private armed followings, not gun ownership generally, so the answer is a qualified 1.

notes: Stated-view record is thin: almost no words of his own survive, so answers rest on statutes and measures he drove, and on Bacon's 1622 history, which is secondhand and late (low at most where it is the only source). Bacon reports a 1485 proclamation promising to end benevolences and unlawful exactions except in ancient cases; the king later raised benevolences, so the budget-needs-parliament answer is mixed. The Navigation Act texts for 1485 and 1489 were not found on the pages opened; the shipping points come from Bacon's account. The 1485 Act of Succession is known from a statute list, not its full text. Many statements (modern welfare, rights, religion in public life, ecology, technology) have no bearing on his record and are null.
